You’re getting the clicks; the blockers are clarity (min‑stay/real rate by dates) and trust (reviews/flexibility) not living where people decide to search.

Here’s the 10‑point shortlist, ordered by speed to impact:

48‑hour fixes
1) Put “Most weekends: 2‑night minimum” visibly on the Rooms page and each room tile; repeat the note next to the date picker.
2) Move “Why book direct” perks to sit beside the date picker and the portal hand‑off; add “Flexible cancellation” in plain words there.
3) Add a reviews strip above the fold: 2–3 recent lines with source badges and a link to the source.
4) Change “From £129 BB” to “From £129 BB (typical midweek)” and swap the CTA on tiles to “View availability” to cue date‑first behaviour.

Two‑week tests
5) If your portal exposes it, surface live availability (and an indicative rate) on room tiles for selected dates; pre‑fill dates on click either way.
6) Show “Only X rooms left for your dates” and “Secure booking, free cancellation” next to the date picker; include your phone number there for last‑minute callers.
7) Booking flow friction: keep people in the same tab, preserve a clear “Back to rooms” link, keep dates pre‑filled, and show a simple progress indicator.

Page structure and UX
8) Room tiles: tighten hierarchy—name, sleeps, breakfast included, 2–3 hero amenities, then price; keep secondary details behind “More info.”
9) Calendar UX: grey out impossible single nights when a 2‑night minimum applies and explain the rule inline so it feels like guidance, not an error.
10) Mobile: compress the hero, make the date picker and CTAs thumb‑sized, and add a sticky “Book now” that carries selected dates across pages.

Measurement to prove it worked
- In your analytics, track a simple funnel: Availability search -> Room tile clicks -> Portal start -> Confirmation. Use it to read where fall‑off improves as you ship the fixes.

If you want, I can share wireframe examples for the room tiles, date picker block, and the reviews strip we’ve used with bookings‑led brands.

sent_subject: Meta GEM: what changed today, how to use it for Fell View’s 3 tests, and how to read lift on mobile
sent:
Maya —

Meta’s new Generative Ads Model (GEM) rolled out today. Meta reports up to +18.9% conversions and +12% CTR from one model optimising creative and placement across FB/IG/Reels; useful, but hotel‑specific lift will depend on the quality of booking signals you feed it.

How to use GEM for Fell View’s 3 ad+landing tests
1) Weekend 2‑night package (pre‑qualify): Ads say “Two‑night Lake District weekend” + key perks (breakfast, late checkout), and state the 2‑night rule up front. Landing: a focused weekend page or variant with Fri–Sun pre‑selected, the 2‑night rule and 2–3 recent reviews beside the date picker, one CTA: Check availability.
2) Midweek direct‑book value: Ads lead with “Midweek 10% direct rate + flexible cancellation + free parking.” Landing: midweek dates pre‑filled, perks and review strip next to the date picker.
3) Dog‑friendly getaway: Ads promise “Dog‑friendly rooms near Ambleside trails.” Landing: dog‑friendly rooms filtered by default, min‑stay made explicit near dates.

Make GEM do the work
- Campaign structure: one consolidated campaign per test with Advantage+ placements; broad targeting; 3–5 creative variants per concept (square + vertical), one promise per ad.
- Conversion signals: ideal is booking confirmations with value back to Meta. If the portal can’t pass that, set portal‑start as the optimisation event and track confirmations separately. If available, include arrival date and length of stay in the signal.
- Creative cues: lead with the room/setting in the first frame and copy that pre‑qualifies (e.g., “Two‑night minimum on weekends”).

How to read lift alongside mobile portal‑starts
- Primary read: Mobile portal‑starts per 100 availability searches, by week, per test page, vs your pre‑test baseline. Secondary: Confirmations per 100 portal‑starts (lagging).
- Sanity check: Compare mobile vs desktop; GEM’s gains should skew mobile.
- Expectation: treat a sustained +5–10% improvement in the mobile portal‑start rate as a meaningful win; Meta’s +18.9% is aggregate, not hotel‑specific.

If helpful, I can share quick wireframes for the three landing variants and a simple tracking map for passing portal‑starts/confirmations back to Meta.
